newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany says employment levels dropped in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Germany says employment levels dropped in 1996.

text.p: The pace of job cuts quickened in 1996 as the number of people working in Germany fell 1.2 percent to 34.5 million workers, underscoring the jobless crisis, the German statistics office said on Monday.

The Wiesbaden office said the number of people working in Germany -- but not necessarily living in Germany -- fell by 404,000 to 34.504 million from 34.909 million in 1995, when the number of people employed slipped 0.4 percent.

In west Germany, the number fell by 1.1 percent to 28.215 million from 28.523 million. The drop was more significant in the east, where the number of employed dropped 1.5 percent to 6.289 million people compared with 6.386 million in 1995.
The loss of jobs in eastern Germany marked a reversal from the 1.1 percent gain in 1995.

The report was issued ahead of Thursday's release of unemployment data for January by the Nuremberg-based German labour office, which was expected to show no improvement from the record unemployment gripping the country.

One German union official said last week she expected the jobless total to rise substantially above 4.4 million for the month compared with the seasonally-adjusted record 4.15 million unemployed in December.

The president of the labour office, Bernhard Jagoda, also said after publication of the December unemployment data that the 4.5 million figure could be reached if the poor weather so far this winter continued up until March.
The Wiesbaden report also said the gap between wages in east and west Germany narrowed last year as wage gains in the east at least more than doubled in manufacturing industry.

Average monthly gross wages of all manufacturing employees in west Germany in July 1996 -- the time-period measured by the office -- rose 1.9 percent to 5,048 marks compared to a gain of five percent to 3,712 marks in the east.
The report said the ratio between east and west salaries rose 73.5 percent in July 1996 from 71.4 percent in July 1995.

Among salaried workers, the report said salaries in the west rose 3.0 percent to 6,369 marks per month compared with a 7.2 percent increase in the east to 4,675 marks, further narrowing the gap to 73.4 percent of western salaries.

Employees in former East Germany were also working longer hours, with the average paid work hours per week in the manufacturing sector up 0.2 percent to 40.3 hours compared with a 2.6 percent drop in the west to 37.9 hours.
